demographics: Prevalence rises steadily with age; about two-thirds of US adults over 60 have hypertension
More common and more severe in non-Hispanic Black adults, who also develop it at younger ages
Men tend to develop it earlier than women; women catch up and exceed men after menopause
Lower socioeconomic status and lower education are associated with higher prevalence
family_history: Hypertension in a parent or sibling
Early cardiovascular disease in a first-degree relative
social_history: High-sodium diet or frequent restaurant meals
exposures: Chronic loud snoring or witnessed apnea in a bed partner

chief_complaints.text: The nurse told me my blood pressure was high at my last checkup
I feel fine — I only came in because my numbers were up
I get headaches and wonder if it's my pressure
My home cuff keeps reading high

hpi.onset: Insidious; found incidentally on a routine visit or screening, or after a mildly elevated reading is repeated
hpi.duration: Usually present for months to years before it is recognized; most patients have no clear start date
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive with age; readings drift upward over years, and many patients are diagnosed only after several elevated readings at separate visits
hpi.location: Not applicable — a whole-body condition measured in the arm
hpi.quality: Asymptomatic; when symptoms occur they are nonspecific (dull headache, fatigue, dizziness)
hpi.severity: Most patients feel entirely well; severity is defined by the blood pressure numbers and by end-organ effects, not by how the patient feels
hpi.timing: Readings are elevated on repeated occasions, at rest, on separate days
aggravating: Missing doses of blood pressure medicine

associated_symptoms.text: Headache, often in the morning or at the back of the head
Chest pain or pressure with exertion

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain at rest or pressure lasting more than a few minutes
Sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body
Sudden severe headache unlike any before
Racing heart with sweating and pounding headaches (spells)
Muscle cramps or weakness from low potassium
Weight loss, fever or night sweats
Swelling of the face, hands or feet with dark urine

argues_against: Vasculitis or another systemic inflammatory illness

negatives: Chest pain that radiates to the back

positives.text: Getting up at night to urinate
Snoring or witnessed pauses in breathing at night

negatives: Episodes of pounding headache, sweating and racing heart
Unexplained weight gain with purple stretch marks

atypical.how_it_differs: Hypertension is uncommon in children and usually secondary to kidney disease, coarctation of the aorta or an endocrine cause; it is detected on routine screening or during workup of another problem, and the child is typically symptom-free.

Isolated systolic hypertension with a wide pulse pressure is typical because arteries stiffen with age; orthostatic drops in pressure and postprandial dizziness are more common, and symptoms may be attributed to aging rather than to blood pressure.

Elevated readings after 20 weeks with proteinuria, swelling or headaches suggest preeclampsia rather than chronic hypertension; blood pressure can fall in early pregnancy and rise again later, so a previously normal reading does not exclude the diagnosis.
The threshold for treatment is lower and target pressures are tighter; hypertension often coexists with diabetic kidney disease, so rising creatinine or protein in the urine may be the first clue.
missing_classic_features: Isolated elevation of blood pressure without kidney involvement

atypical.how_it_differs: Often accompanied by obstructive sleep apnea, so daytime sleepiness, loud snoring and morning headaches are more prominent; weight loss alone can lower pressure substantially.
Hypertension is frequently secondary to chronic kidney disease and is harder to control; patients may have swelling, fatigue and abnormal kidney labs rather than an isolated high reading.
missing_classic_features: Easy blood pressure control with one medicine

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; often overweight; comfortable at rest
general.moderate: Well-appearing but may be overweight with central adiposity; no acute distress
general.severe: May appear anxious or mildly uncomfortable; possible signs of chronic end-organ strain (mild dyspnea on exertion, ankle edema)
general.critical: Ill-appearing with signs of acute end-organ injury — severe headache, confusion, chest pain, dyspnea, focal neurologic deficits, or visual disturbance

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with the patient seated quietly for 5 minutes, using an appropriately sized cuff at heart level
findings.finding: Elevated systolic and/or diastolic pressure, confirmed on repeat measurement

findings.maneuver: Repeat the blood pressure after 5 minutes of quiet rest and again at a separate visit
findings.finding: Persistently elevated readings on separate occasions

findings.maneuver: Compare blood pressure in both arms
findings.finding: Interarm difference less than 10 mm Hg

findings.maneuver: Compare blood pressure in both arms
findings.finding: Interarm systolic difference of 10 mm Hg or more, suggesting peripheral arterial disease or aortic coarctation
Arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, or flame hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots in severe cases
Blurring of the optic disc margins (papilledema), indicating malignant hypertension

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex with the bell
findings.finding: Fourth heart sound (S4), reflecting a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle
Laterally displaced and sustained apical impulse from left ventricular hypertrophy
Carotid bruit, suggesting atherosclerotic narrowing

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular venous pulsation at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure, suggesting heart failure
Bibasilar crackles, suggesting pulmonary edema from hypertensive heart failure

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of each foot and the lower shins
findings.finding: Pitting edema, suggesting heart failure or kidney disease

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the epigastrium and both upper quadrants for a bruit
findings.finding: Systolic-diastolic bruit in the epigastrium or flank, suggesting renal artery stenosis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the flanks and abdomen for masses
findings.finding: Palpable enlarged kidneys, suggesting polycystic kidney disease

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial and femoral pulses simultaneously
findings.finding: Diminished or delayed femoral pulses, suggesting coarctation of the aorta

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including strength, sensation, speech and gait
findings.finding: No focal deficits

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation, attention and level of consciousness
findings.finding: Alert and oriented, no confusion

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for striae, bruising, xanthomas and acanthosis nigricans
findings.finding: No violaceous striae, no xanthomas, no acanthosis nigricans
No goiter or nodule

labs.caveat: Fasting glucose screens for diabetes and prediabetes, which are common companions of primary hypertension and change the treatment target.
Values of 5.7–6.4% indicate prediabetes and 6.5% or higher diabetes; either lowers the threshold for drug treatment.

A rise in creatinine suggests chronic kidney disease as a cause or consequence of hypertension; a creatinine bump of more than 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB points to renal artery stenosis.
Spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia should raise suspicion for primary aldosteronism.
Mild hyponatremia can accompany syndrome of inappropriate ADH or adrenal insufficiency.
Low bicarbonate suggests a metabolic acidosis from advanced kidney disease or a secondary endocrine cause.
Part of global cardiovascular risk estimation; hyperlipidemia commonly coexists with hypertension.
Low HDL is part of the metabolic syndrome that frequently accompanies primary hypertension.
Proteinuria suggests hypertensive or diabetic kidney damage and worsens cardiovascular risk.
Hematuria with proteinuria and rising creatinine suggests glomerulonephritis rather than uncomplicated hypertension.
RBC casts point to glomerulonephritis; muddy-brown casts point to acute tubular injury.
Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can raise blood pressure; a suppressed TSH suggests hyperthyroidism as a secondary cause.
An elevated morning cortisol is a screening clue to Cushing syndrome; confirm with a 24-hour urine free cortisol or overnight dexamethasone suppression test.
Negative. Mandatory in anyone who could be pregnant before starting an ACE inhibitor, ARB or thiazide and before any imaging that uses radiation.

findings.finding: Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria (S in V1 plus R in V5 or V6 greater than 35 mm, or R in aVL greater than 11 mm)
Downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in a strain pattern
Peaked, symmetric T waves suggesting hyperkalemia
Atrial fibrillation
Left bundle branch block or nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay
Left atrial enlargement (broad, notched P waves in lead II and a deep terminal negative component in V1)

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, or a murmur

findings.text: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with increased wall thickness
Diastolic dysfunction with impaired relaxation (grade I)
Left atrial enlargement
Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (hypertensive cardiomyopathy)
Aortic valve sclerosis or stenosis

imaging.preferred_when: Resistant hypertension, an abdominal bruit, or a creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB

findings.text: Elevated peak systolic velocity in the renal artery suggesting stenosis
Tardus-parvus waveform downstream of a stenosis
Asymmetric kidney size

imaging.study: CT angiography of the renal arteries
imaging.preferred_when: When duplex ultrasound is nondiagnostic and renal artery stenosis is strongly suspected

findings.text: Focal narrowing at the ostium or proximal renal artery (atherosclerotic stenosis)
String-of-beads appearance suggesting fibromuscular dysplasia

imaging.study: Magnetic resonance angiography of the renal arteries
imaging.preferred_when: When iodinated contrast or radiation must be avoided

findings.text: Renal artery narrowing or a string-of-beads pattern

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected aortic coarctation or aortic dissection

findings.text: Narrowing of the aortic isthmus just distal to the left subclavian artery (coarctation)
Intimal flap dividing the aortic lumen (dissection)
Extensive collateral intercostal arteries

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease or an adrenal mass

findings.text: Multiple bilateral renal cysts of varying size
Enlarged kidneys with a bosselated contour
Adrenal nodule or hyperplasia

imaging.study: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary

findings.text: Pituitary microadenoma
Cardiomegaly with a left ventricular contour
Rib notching from collateral vessels (coarctation)
Pulmonary vascular congestion or edema (hypertensive heart failure)

initial.why: Baseline potassium, sodium, bicarbonate and creatinine before starting a diuretic or renin-angiotensin blocker
Screens for anemia or polycythemia that can accompany kidney disease
Fasting lipid panel for global cardiovascular risk estimation
Screens for diabetes and prediabetes, which change the treatment threshold
Thyroid disease is a treatable secondary cause of hypertension
Proteinuria, hematuria or casts point to kidney disease as a cause or consequence
Rules out pregnancy before starting an ACE inhibitor, ARB or thiazide
Assesses left ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic function and ejection fraction
initial.only_if: there is a murmur, signs of heart failure, or an abnormal ECG
hypertension is resistant, an abdominal bruit is heard, or creatinine rises after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB

initial.test: CT angiography of the renal arteries
initial.why: Confirms renal artery stenosis when ultrasound is nondiagnostic
initial.only_if: renal artery stenosis is strongly suspected and duplex ultrasound is inconclusive

confirmatory.why: Confirms sustained hypertension and excludes white-coat hypertension when office readings are borderline or discordant with home readings
Multiple readings at home confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment

supporting.only_if: central obesity, purple striae, proximal weakness or unexplained hypokalemia is present

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
supporting.why: Looks for polycystic kidneys or an adrenal mass
supporting.only_if: flank masses, a family history of polycystic kidney disease, or an adrenal nodule is suspected

supporting.test: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary

supporting.only_if: there is an arm-to-leg blood pressure gradient, diminished femoral pulses, or tearing chest pain

not_indicated.why: No role in the routine evaluation of hypertension
Not part of the hypertension workup unless there is shock or sepsis
Rarely changes management in uncomplicated hypertension

decision_points: Confirm elevated readings on at least two separate visits before labeling hypertension; use home or ambulatory monitoring when office values are borderline or discordant.
Screen every newly diagnosed patient for target-organ damage and for clues to a secondary cause.
Check a pregnancy test before prescribing an ACE inhibitor, ARB or thiazide, and before any imaging that uses radiation.
A blood pressure of 180/120 mm Hg or higher with signs of acute end-organ injury is a hypertensive emergency and needs immediate treatment, not an outpatient workup.
Resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on three drugs including a diuretic) should prompt a search for secondary causes and for medication nonadherence.

criteria.name: ACC/AHA blood pressure categories
criteria.summary: Normal is below 120/80 mm Hg; elevated is 120–129 systolic with diastolic below 80; stage 1 hypertension is 130–139 systolic or 80–89 diastolic; stage 2 hypertension is 140 or higher systolic or 90 or higher diastolic; a hypertensive crisis is above 180 systolic and/or above 120 diastolic.
items: Elevated: 120–129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic
Stage 2 hypertension: 140 or higher systolic or 90 or higher diastolic
Hypertensive crisis: above 180 systolic and/or above 120 diastolic

differential.name: White-coat hypertension
differential.why_considered: Office readings are elevated but the patient feels well and home readings are normal

history: Home or workplace readings are consistently normal
Anxiety around medical visits
No symptoms and no end-organ complaints
exam: Elevated office blood pressure that falls with repeated measurement and quiet rest
labs: Normal basic metabolic panel, urinalysis and lipid panel
imaging: Normal echocardiogram without left ventricular hypertrophy

differential.name: Primary aldosteronism
differential.why_considered: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic-induced low potassium
differential.trigger: Hypokalemia that is spontaneous or persists after stopping diuretics, or hypertension resistant to three drugs

history: Hypertension requiring three or more medicines
Muscle cramps, weakness or palpitations from low potassium
Early onset hypertension or a family history of early hypertension
exam: Blood pressure that remains high despite multiple drugs
labs: Elevated plasma aldosterone with suppressed renin activity
imaging: Adrenal nodule or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia on CT

differential.name: Renal artery stenosis
differential.why_considered: Resistant or abruptly worsening hypertension, especially with an abdominal bruit
differential.trigger: Creatinine rise of more than 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a new abdominal bruit

history: Hypertension that was previously controlled and is now difficult
Flash pulmonary edema
Atherosclerotic disease elsewhere
exam: Systolic-diastolic bruit in the epigastrium or flank
labs: Rising creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
imaging: Elevated peak systolic velocity on renal artery duplex ultrasound
Focal ostial narrowing on CT or MR angiography

differential.name: Chronic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Hypertension with abnormal kidney labs, proteinuria or edema

history: Long-standing diabetes or known kidney disease
Foamy urine or swelling
Fatigue and poor appetite
exam: Hypertension that is difficult to control
labs: Elevated creatinine with reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate
Anemia and hyperkalemia in advanced disease

differential.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
differential.why_considered: Hypertension with loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness

history: Loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing
Morning headaches and unrefreshing sleep
Daytime sleepiness
exam: Obesity with a large neck circumference
imaging: Polysomnography showing apneas and hypopneas with oxygen desaturation

differential.name: Thyroid disease
differential.why_considered: Hypertension with palpitations, weight change or heat intolerance

history: Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tremor
Or weight gain, cold intolerance and fatigue in hypothyroidism
exam: Tachycardia, tremor, warm moist skin, goiter
Or bradycardia, dry skin and delayed reflexes
labs: Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 in hyperthyroidism
Elevated TSH with low free T4 in hypothyroidism

differential.name: Pheochromocytoma
differential.why_considered: Paroxysmal hypertension with spells of headache, sweating and racing heart
differential.trigger: Episodic pounding headache with sweating and tachycardia, or marked blood pressure variability

history: Sudden spells of severe headache, palpitations and drenching sweats
Spells triggered by stress, exercise or abdominal pressure
Family history of endocrine tumors
labs: Elevated plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine metanephrines
imaging: Adrenal mass on CT or MRI
Increased uptake on MIBG or DOTATATE imaging

differential.name: Cushing syndrome
differential.why_considered: Hypertension with central obesity, purple striae and proximal weakness

history: Weight gain around the trunk with thin arms and legs
Easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness
Use of glucocorticoid medications
exam: Moon facies and dorsocervical fat pad
labs: Elevated late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urine free cortisol
Failure to suppress cortisol on overnight dexamethasone suppression test
imaging: Adrenal nodule or hyperplasia on CT

differential.name: Coarctation of the aorta
differential.why_considered: Hypertension in a young patient with upper-limb hypertension and weak leg pulses
differential.trigger: Arm-to-leg blood pressure gradient or diminished femoral pulses in a young patient

history: Hypertension diagnosed at a young age
Leg fatigue or cramping with exercise
Known congenital heart disease
exam: Systolic murmur over the back or left infraclavicular area
imaging: Narrowing of the aortic isthmus on CT or MR angiography
Rib notching on chest x-ray from collateral vessels

differential.name: Medication-induced hypertension
differential.why_considered: Elevated readings that began or worsened after starting a new medication

history: Recent use of NSAIDs, decongestants, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, stimulants or calcineurin inhibitors
Temporal relationship between the drug and rising readings
Alcohol or licorice use
exam: Elevated blood pressure without other specific findings
labs: Normal basic metabolic panel and urinalysis

severity.mild: Stage 1 hypertension: systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89 mm Hg, no symptoms, no target-organ damage
severity.moderate: Stage 2 hypertension: systolic 140–159 or diastolic 90–99 mm Hg, possible early target-organ changes such as left ventricular hypertrophy
severity.severe: Systolic 160–179 or diastolic 100–119 mm Hg, often with target-organ strain such as retinopathy, diastolic dysfunction or proteinuria
severity.critical: Hypertensive crisis: systolic above 180 and/or diastolic above 120 mm Hg; with acute end-organ injury this is a hypertensive emergency requiring immediate treatment

red_flags.finding: Blood pressure above 180/120 mm Hg with chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic deficit or visual change
red_flags.meaning: Hypertensive emergency with acute end-organ injury; needs immediate treatment

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe headache unlike any before
red_flags.meaning: Possible intracerebral hemorrhage or hypertensive encephalopathy

red_flags.finding: Focal weakness, numbness, slurred speech or vision loss
red_flags.meaning: Possible stroke or transient ischemic attack
Malignant hypertension; requires urgent blood pressure control

red_flags.finding: New confusion or reduced level of consciousness
red_flags.meaning: Hypertensive encephalopathy or another acute neurologic emergency

red_flags.finding: Pulmonary edema with crackles and hypoxemia
red_flags.meaning: Hypertensive heart failure; needs urgent treatment
Suggests primary aldosteronism or another secondary cause

complications.name: Heart failure with preserved or reduced ejection fraction
Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction

special_populations.differences: Hypertension is uncommon and usually secondary to kidney disease, coarctation of the aorta or an endocrine cause; diagnosis uses age-, height- and sex-specific percentiles, and the child is typically symptom-free.

Isolated systolic hypertension with a wide pulse pressure is typical because arteries stiffen with age; orthostatic and postprandial drops in pressure are more common, and treatment must avoid excessive lowering that causes falls.

Elevated readings after 20 weeks with proteinuria, swelling or headaches suggest preeclampsia rather than chronic hypertension; ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazides are avoided, and blood pressure can fall in early pregnancy and rise again later.
The threshold for treatment is lower and target pressures are tighter; hypertension often coexists with diabetic kidney disease, so rising creatinine or protein in the urine may be the first clue.
Often accompanied by obstructive sleep apnea, so daytime sleepiness, loud snoring and morning headaches are more prominent; weight loss alone can lower pressure substantially.

Hypertension is frequently secondary to chronic kidney disease and is harder to control; patients may have swelling, fatigue and abnormal kidney labs rather than an isolated high reading, and creatinine must be monitored after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

key_questions.question: What were your blood pressure readings, and where were they taken?
key_questions.looking_for: Repeated office readings of 130/80 mm Hg or higher, or home readings that are consistently elevated; a single high reading is not enough

key_questions.question: How long have your pressures been high, and when were they first noted?
key_questions.looking_for: Months to years of elevated readings; a recent abrupt rise suggests a secondary cause

key_questions.question: Do you have any symptoms at all — headaches, dizziness, chest pain, shortness of breath, vision changes?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually none; the presence of chest pain, dyspnea, focal neurologic symptoms or visual loss suggests end-organ injury

key_questions.question: Do you check your blood pressure at home, and what do those readings show?
key_questions.looking_for: Home readings that confirm or refute office values; normal home readings suggest white-coat hypertension

key_questions.question: Are you taking any blood pressure medicine, and have you been able to take it as prescribed?
key_questions.looking_for: Current regimen, doses, adherence, and whether the patient has missed doses

key_questions.question: Do you take any over-the-counter pain relievers, decongestants, or other medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs, pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, stimulants, or other agents that raise blood pressure

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have kidney disease, diabetes, or sleep apnea?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that are causes or consequences of hypertension and that change treatment targets

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have high blood pressure, early heart disease, or kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: A strong family history supports primary hypertension; early cardiovascular disease or polycystic kidney disease suggests other causes

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and do you use tobacco or any stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy or regular alcohol use, tobacco, or stimulant use that contributes to elevated pressure

key_questions.question: How much salt do you eat, and how often do you exercise?
key_questions.looking_for: High dietary sodium and physical inactivity — modifiable contributors

key_questions.question: Do you snore loudly or has anyone seen you stop breathing at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Obstructive sleep apnea, a common secondary contributor

key_questions.question: Have you had spells of pounding headache with sweating and a racing heart?
Have you had sudden weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or loss of vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Stroke or transient ischemic attack — an emergency

key_questions.question: Have you had tearing chest or back pain, or chest pressure with exertion?
key_questions.looking_for: Aortic dissection or acute coronary syndrome

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy must be excluded before starting an ACE inhibitor, ARB or thiazide, and before imaging that uses radiation

reasoning_points: Elevated blood pressure confirmed on repeated readings at separate visits, or by home or ambulatory monitoring
The patient is usually asymptomatic, so the diagnosis rests on the numbers rather than on symptoms
Office readings are interpreted against the ACC/AHA categories: normal below 120/80, elevated 120–129 systolic, stage 1 130–139 or 80–89, stage 2 140 or higher or 90 or higher
A search for target-organ damage: left ventricular hypertrophy, retinopathy, kidney impairment, proteinuria, vascular disease
A search for secondary causes when the presentation is atypical: young age, resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, abdominal bruit, spells, or a creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Medications and substances that raise blood pressure are reviewed and, where possible, stopped
Global cardiovascular risk is estimated from lipids, glucose or A1c, smoking and kidney function
Pregnancy is excluded before prescribing an ACE inhibitor, ARB or thiazide
A blood pressure above 180/120 mm Hg with signs of acute end-organ injury is a hypertensive emergency, not an outpatient workup

easy: Middle-aged or older adult with repeated office readings of 150/95 mm Hg
No symptoms and no target-organ damage
Overweight, high-sodium diet, family history of hypertension
Basic metabolic panel, urinalysis and lipids are unremarkable
medium: Borderline office readings with normal home readings — white-coat hypertension must be excluded
Patient on an NSAID or decongestant that is raising the pressure
Coexisting diabetes or chronic kidney disease that changes the treatment target
Mild left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG or echocardiogram
hard: Young patient with severe hypertension and hypokalemia suggesting primary aldosteronism
Resistant hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic
Abdominal bruit or a creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor suggesting renal artery stenosis
Paroxysmal spells of headache, sweating and tachycardia suggesting pheochromocytoma
Young patient with weak femoral pulses and an arm-to-leg gradient suggesting coarctation of the aorta
Blood pressure above 180/120 mm Hg with chest pain, dyspnea or a focal neurologic deficit — a hypertensive emergency
